Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

Varun Agrawal, Ayush Srivastava, Eshan Gujar, Kaushal Kumar, Ayush Gupta

We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

Probabilistic safety judges return the probability of a safety label and cheaply score reinforcement learning rollouts. A confidence gate sends only uncertain verdicts to a stronger LLM judge, which leaves confidently passed harm in a blind spot. Policies can exploit this blind spot, and commercial judges release new versions. We propose a protocol that validates such a judge before and during training, separates the share of confidently passed harm from its amount, and re-validates it after each judge change. We apply it to two versions of Jev, a commercial decision-only judge, and to an open guard classifier. Under the probability reward of Jev, passed harm shrinks in all 11 runs under the primary reference, mostly more slowly than caught harm, and concentrates in the blind spot. Binarizing this judge meets the escape criterion on Llama, and the open guard classifier shows an escape signal in one seed under a second reference. Guard classifiers share this blind spot, and even frontier LLM judges catch at most one of 10 human-labeled confident misses. Without a trained reward model, the probability reward with a helpfulness term lowers HarmBench attack success on Llama-3.1-8B from 0.287 to at most 0.033 at the final checkpoint.

☆ Navital Gym: Rule-Graded Agent Environments for Indian Workflows
Daksh Bathla
AI agents are being deployed on Indian workflows such as payments, tax, forms, travel and customer support in Hindi and Hinglish. Public agent evaluations rarely cover these workflows, and many score with another language model. We present Navital Gym, a set of six open environments with 321 public tasks in five task families: trip planning, UPI payments and disputes, GST invoicing and returns, form filling (including a multi-document split) and customer support in Hindi, Hinglish and three experimental Indian languages. Every task is graded by named, deterministic rules that recompute the outcome from a synthetic sandbox world. No language model judges any score. We report one run per task for three models on all six environments, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and for Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite on two (UPI and the Support core). Opus solves 315 of 321 tasks, Sonnet 302 and Haiku 205. Trip planning and Hindi/Hinglish support separate the models most. We also describe a private held-out set that is not published, and a 7B adapter trained in the gym. Code is Apache-2.0 and task data is CC BY 4.0. The rules are a documented simplification of Indian practice, not the live systems.

☆ Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
Zhen Xu, Hang Yin, Zitao Zhang, Kevin Zhao, Xuefeng Liu
Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

Multi-agent self-improvement enables agents to improve through interaction and feedback. However, sequential dependencies across agents and refinement rounds can propagate errors, increase computational costs, and limit parallelism. Moreover, refining individual features or agents in isolation can overlook their dependencies and restrict collective coordination. To address these challenges, we propose ConvRSI, a framework for parallelizing multi-agent self-improvement through convolution. ConvRSI couples intra-agent convolution, which jointly refines related agent features, with inter-agent graph convolution, which aggregates messages according to the collaboration topology. Both stages operate in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeatedly decoding and re-encoding intermediate messages. Experiments on MATH-500 show that ConvRSI achieves 5.04% performance improvement while reducing 17.27% inference cost, and 45.11% latency compared with RecursiveMAS. It also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing their topologies as adjacency matrices. These results demonstrate the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. Our code and datasets are provided in https://github.com/LYA2333/ConvRSI.

These rhetorical roles often intertwine and shift sentence by sentence, making reliable classification difficult. This paper introduces the first sentence-level annotated dataset of Dutch judicial decisions, labelled across four legally meaningful categories: material facts, submissions, judicial reasoning, and the court's decision, alongside non-annotated (None) content, and compares several classification strategies, including a staged pipeline that separates None detection from the rhetorical roles, and a Bayesian update that leverages information about the section-header a sentence belongs to. Our results show that no single strategy dominates on both precision and recall: header priors help most when the None sentences are excluded and offer little benefit for None detection itself. These trade-offs matter in practice. For instance, extractive summarisation depends more on recall so it does not miss relevant facts, whereas outcome prediction depends more on precision regarding decision and facts sentences so that the predicted ruling is not contaminated by noise. We use these trade-offs and map the approaches tested in this study onto a set of representative legal NLP use cases.

Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

We lead with that because the usual summary of a multilingual result -- a percentage-point drop from English -- does not say whether what survives the drop is performance at all. On a paired English--Hausa set of \NEval{} MedMCQA items, three instruction-tuned models of 3--4B parameters lose between \GapMedGemma{} and \GapQwen{} points of accuracy, every gap significant after Holm correction. Back-translating the Hausa items into English recovers between half and two-thirds of the gap for the two general-purpose models but not demonstrably for the medically adapted one, so the deficit is substantially, though not wholly, a matter of the language of presentation. Answers are also far less stable: agreement across three option orderings falls from \ConsEnQwen{} to \ConsHaQwen{} in the worst case. An exploratory error analysis of \ENRows{} discordant items attributes most of the damage to medical vocabulary lost in translation (\ETerm{}, 95\% CI \ETermLo{}--\ETermHi{}), usually in the question stem. A fourth registered hypothesis proposed closing the gap with self-generated preference pairs. Its pilot gate found nothing to train on: asked to reason in Hausa rather than to pick a letter, the model echoes the prompt back, switches into Swahili, or simply stops without answering; only \GateParse{} of chains are parseable. We report that intervention as not run, which is itself the sharper result -- a forced-choice benchmark cannot see a model that has no generative command of the language at all. All hypotheses, thresholds and decision rules were registered before any model was run, and all deviations are logged.

☆ CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation

Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

☆ Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
Manan Suri, Dinesh Manocha
Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.

First, reuse never avoids re-encoding: if migration must complete, every strategy eventually encodes every document; reuse only changes when that work is paid and the quality served meanwhile. Second, adapters should be compared with the old model, not only the new one. Of five adapter variants, only same-family LLM bridges beat the old model, and only by a negligible margin. Third, window re-ranking cost can be priced from the old index alone; pre-registered replays on all 8,841,823 passages confirmed the prediction on all three tested pairs. Workload skew also matters: across 36 further pre-registered Zipf replays, the planned family matched on 32. These findings yield three pre-migration rules: whether reuse is worthwhile, which strategy to use, and how deep a window to take. The depth rule priced every window that reached target quality to within 4 parts in 10^5 of the corpus. On NQ, a pre-committed plan selected the family on 10 of 11 pairs and priced every window exactly. Quality inputs transferred less reliably across corpus scale, so the model gap and window quality loss must be measured on the serving index.

☆ Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
Roman Makarov, Zhe Xu, Jian Kang
Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. Our code is available at https://github.com/rmakarovv/fast-at-the-frontier.

Second, we find that group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record, and that even then the models' group differences rest more on the demographic label in the prompt than on the individual respondent, which the usual check of reproducing known group differences does not reveal. Third, we find that the models make groups look more alike than they are, keeping differences in circumstances while flattening or reversing differences in attitudes, most sharply for religious affiliation and ethnic origin, both special categories of personal data. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Language models are dynamical systems. A transformer is iterated over its layers, over the steps of its training and over the tokens it generates, and on each of these three clocks it shows behavior that nonlinear dynamics has studied for a century: fixed points, bifurcations, synchronization, chaos and noise-driven escape from potential wells. The two communities rarely meet, so this behavior is often rediscovered under new names. We build a bridge between them. To describe, we condense about 200 papers into the Three-Clock Dictionary, which maps fifteen concepts of nonlinear dynamics onto each clock and marks every correspondence as proved, measured or conjectured, and we show each concept in a mechanical system and in a language model side by side. To explain, we derive reduced-order models: the softmax is a Boltzmann distribution, gradient descent an Euler step on a nonlinear spring, a loss spike a ball thrown out of a stiff valley, attention on the circle a Kuramoto model, and a repetition loop a well that deepens while it is occupied. We then test these explanations on open language models, on a laptop CPU. Escape from repetition loops in GPT-2 and Pythia follows the Arrhenius law with the logit gap as the barrier, and the barrier deepens and then saturates, so the temperature needed to leave a loop falls like $1/\ln N$ with the generation length $N$ and rises with model size. Coherent text lives in a narrow window of temperatures, which a small reasoning model shares at its recommended temperature. Training makes each Pythia layer more expansive, and a small transformer trains at a multi-mode edge of stability. The third step, solving problems of language models, is still ahead: controllers derived from the escape analysis remove loops but do not yet beat the best fixed temperature. We state twelve open problems where nonlinear dynamics could get there.

Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. We introduce Solver2System, a dataset of PDE solvers with multiple representations, controlled corruptions, and lexical perturbations, to evaluate whether LLMs can recover the underlying physical system through (1) cross-representation consistency and (2) static and agentic detection of physical invalidity. Across eight open-weight models, LLMs systematically favor some representations when evidence conflicts, and lexical perturbations to code alter interpretation of other unchanged representations. Execution improves physical-validity judgments, but weaker agents can judge correctly without identifying the causal defect. Thus, LLMs may reach correct judgments despite inconsistent representation reconciliation or causal misdiagnosis.

A reasoning model that has reached a correct answer can lose it by continuing to think. Deciding whether to stop means comparing two probabilities at the same point of a chain: that the answer the model would give if stopped now is correct (its commitment), and that the answer it will finish with is correct (its verdict). We show that the verdict alone, which is what final-correctness probes estimate, cannot make this comparison. As a forecast of a fixed outcome it has no predictable drift, whether continuing helps or hurts. The commitment-verdict gap equals the expected remaining change in answer quality and the accuracy gained by stopping. A second identity splits any accuracy-versus-budget curve into answer change within chains and change in which chains are still running. We measure both on MATH-500. At all 379 points where DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B holds a correct answer, selected without regard to how its chain ends, continuing loses 3.6 points on average (95% CI [2.2, 5.2]), and the loss concentrates in a few problems. In six reasoning models from three families, on MATH-500 and OlympiadBench and with budgets up to 16,384 tokens, declining accuracy curves come from which chains remain, while the chains still reasoning keep or improve their answers. An oracle stopping rule gains at most +1.8 and +2.5 points at 1.5B and 7B. The framework says what to measure before building a stopping rule.

Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. Experiments that change one condition at a time agree with this hypothesis. When Baton is trained on every token, however, its accuracy on these questions rises and then declines. We further split the gradient of the next-token loss into three terms. Removing the two terms that depend on the particular training set raises the peak accuracy but does not remove the decline. The decline arises in the second hop while the model still recalls both facts.

Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. All our results come from one object: a pair is valid for every member of a finite family exactly when its points lie in antipodal cells of the family's membership map. On finite classes, generation fails exactly when a family that shares a presentation has a finite common support; on countable classes this finite condition no longer suffices. (3) On clean data the four learning criteria form a strict diamond. (4) Under corruption the order changes: some classes are identifiable from contrastive pairs under every finite budget by one algorithm, but not from positive examples with one corrupted example.

We study private language identification and generation in the agnostic statistical setting. For identification, privacy is free: at every fixed $\varepsilon$, pure DP and $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP with $δ\ge n^{-O(1)}$ keep the non-private rate $\exp(-r(n))$ for every $r(n)=o(n)$. For generation, the price depends on what is public. With a public witness bound, pure DP loses at most a factor $Θ(\min\{1,\varepsilon\})$ in the exponent, and on suitable two-language collections the optimal rate is $\exp(-Θ(\min\{1,\varepsilon\}\,n))$. Without such a bound, pure DP can lose the exponential rate itself, already for two languages: every rate $\exp(-o(n))$ stays achievable, but no exponential rate is. On these collections, $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP keeps an exponential rate if and only if $\log(1/δ)=o(n)$. Three facts about pure DP drive the proofs. It turns a robustness margin into an exponentially small error. It obeys a private form of Le Cam's two-point bound. And it cannot see the absence of a string.

We evaluate Revela on domain-specific (CoIR), reasoning-intensive (BRIGHT), and general-domain (BEIR) benchmarks across various retriever backbones. Without annotated or synthetic query-document pairs, Revela surpasses larger supervised models and proprietary APIs on both CoIR and BRIGHT. It achieves BEIR's unsupervised SoTA with ~1000x less training data and 10x less compute. Performance increases with batch size and model size, highlighting Revela's scalability and its promise for self-supervised retriever learning.

♻ ☆ Guideline-Based Medical Reasoning in LLMs ML4H 2026
Michael Staniek, Artem Sokolov, Stefan Riezler
Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at medical question-answering, yet progress toward medical reasoning models is limited by the lack of scalable, trustworthy reasoning supervision. We propose tapping into the so far underused resource of medical consensus guidelines. These map numerical clinical measurements to disease scores and can optionally be curated for site-specific exceptions. Automatically generating gold-standard reasoning chains from consensus rules enables both large-scale supervised fine-tuning and automatic evaluation. Applying SOFA, SAPS-II, and Sepsis-3 guidelines to MIMIC-III, we show that small fine-tuned models significantly outperform larger one-shot prompted models in derivation correctness and F1 score, achieving near-perfect deductive inference and reliable exception handling. Trustworthy step-by-step reasoning does not reliably emerge from one-shot prompting, even when models receive the consensus definition and an example. Performance across all models declines when forecasting future clinical variables, indicating that, on the evaluated structured ICU tasks, the central challenge is not rule application, but the orthogonal problem of generalizing into the future for prognostic reasoning.
comment: v2: camera-ready version, accepted at ML4H 2026; title changed
♻ ☆ Breaking the Silence: A Dataset and Benchmark for Bangla Text-to-Gloss Translation
Sharif Mohammad Abdullah, Abhijit Paul, Shubhashis Roy Dipta, Zarif Masud, Shebuti Rayana, Ahmedul Kabir
Gloss is a written approximation that bridges Sign Language (SL) and its corresponding spoken language. Despite a deaf and hard-of-hearing population of at least 3 million in Bangladesh, Bangla Sign Language (BdSL) remains largely understudied, with very limited prior work on Bangla text-to-gloss translation and no publicly available parallel dataset at the time of this work. To address this gap, we construct the first publicly available Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, consisting of 1,000 manually annotated and 4,000 synthetically generated Bangla sentence-gloss pairs, along with 159 expert human-annotated pairs used as a test set. Our experimental framework performs a comparative analysis between several fine-tuned open-source models and a leading closed-source LLM to evaluate their performance in low-resource BdSL translation. GPT-5.4 achieves the best automatic metric scores, while open-source models perform competitively despite being much smaller. This work introduces the first publicly available expert-annotated Bangla text-to-gloss dataset, benchmark and trained model for Bangla text-to-gloss translation. It also demonstrates the effectiveness of systematically generated synthetic data for addressing challenges in low-resource sign language translation.
♻ ☆ ViSAR: Training-Free Adaptive-$k$ Retrieval for Document Visual Question Answering
Adrien Mialland, Marc Plantevit, Julien Gallois, Céline Robardet
Document Visual Question Answering (DocVQA) often leverages Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), where late-interaction encoders are commonly used to identify document pages relevant to a user query, before answer generation by a Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM). Existing approaches typically retrieve a fixed top-$k$ number of pages regardless of query complexity, which increases LVLM latency and may degrade answer accuracy when fewer pages would be enough. We introduce ViSAR (Visual Semantic Activation Retrieval), a training-free, budget-aware adaptive-$k$ retrieval method for late-interaction visual document retrieval. ViSAR operates directly in the embedding space to construct a query-conditioned page-level similarity matrix that highlights query-relevant semantics and dynamically determines the number of pages to retrieve, within a given page budget. We evaluate our method across multiple datasets, encoders, and LVLMs. ViSAR retrieves compact, query-adapted page sets that reduce end-to-end RAG latency by up to 58.9\%, with no statistically significant accuracy loss and significant gains in several settings, compared with fixed top-$k$ and adaptive retrieval heuristics. Furthermore, we show that the similarity matrix structure correlates with answer accuracy, suggesting future directions for retrieval quality-aware document understanding.

♻ ☆ SearchJev: A Calibrated System-1 Model for Search Agents
Congfeng Cao, Lipeng Zuo, Konstantinos Papakostas, Qiwei Xu, Songwei Xu, Qianru Meng, Lun Zhou, Zhaochun Ren, Yougang Lyu, Xiaohui Yan
Search agents repeatedly make short decisions about relevance, evidence sufficiency, and search actions. Using generative language models for these decisions introduces latency and unreliable confidence. We present SearchJev, a calibrated System-1 model that separates search decisions from System-2 reasoning and generation. Given a search state and a decision schema, SearchJev scores legal options without autoregressive output generation. We propose Soft-Label Learning for Calibrated Decisions (SLCD) to learn decision probabilities from uncertain supervision and improve the reliability of decision confidence. In a dual-system search agent, SearchJev handles short decisions and delegates uncertain judgments to System 2, which retains planning, query generation, and answer composition. We also introduce SearchDecision-Bench, a benchmark unifying six types of search decisions for training and evaluation. On SearchDecision-Bench, SearchJev improves decision quality over same-size Qwen3.5 autoregressive models, achieves 5.2-5.3 times faster decisions, and reduces average expected calibration error by 41-74%. On BrowseComp-Plus, the dual-system agents achieve a 3.7-4.7 times speedup in active search time while improving answer accuracy from 45% to up to 54%.
♻ ☆ The Granularity Axis: A Micro-to-Macro Latent Direction for Social Roles in Language Models
Chonghan Qin, Xiachong Feng, Ziyun Song, Xiaocheng Feng, Jing Xiong, Lingpeng Kong
Large language models (LLMs) are prompted to adopt social roles from individuals to institutions, but whether their representations encode this difference in social granularity remains unclear. We discover a contrast-based Granularity Axis, the difference between mean macro- and micro-role hidden states, that aligns with the dominant geometry of role space: in Qwen3-8B, its cosine with PC1 is $0.972$, and PC1 explains $52.6\%$ of the variance. Across 75 roles at five levels, with 90,000 role-conditioned and 1,200 default responses per model, projections increase monotonically and remain stable across layers, prompts, and response-quality filters. The structure transfers to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and scales to Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, whose PC1 shares are $45.99\%$ and $31.23\%$. Independent five-rater validation ($α=0.961$) preserves the ordering; identical continuations and affect/formality controls confirm scale-related variation beyond generated wording. The axis is also behaviorally causal: positive steering moves Llama from $2.00$ to $3.17$ on a five-point macro scale for prompts admitting local responses. Steering strength and stability depend on the model's default operating regime. Together, these findings establish social granularity as a representational primitive: a continuous, ordered, causally manipulable direction organizing role-conditioned generation across model families.

♻ ☆ Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization
Zhengyu Hu, Zheyuan Xiao, Yike Wang, Hamish Ivison, Haoyu Wang, Yige Yuan, Rulin Shao, Yuetai Li, Niqi Lyu, Yicheng Ding, Shu Yang, Zhichen Zeng, Banghua Zhu, Jiaxin Pei, Kaize Ding, Pradeep Dasigi, Dan Roth, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, Teng Xiao, Radha Poovendran
In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
♻ ☆ HandwritingAgent: Language-Driven Handwriting Synthesis in Scalable Vector Space
Jaward Sesay, Yue Yu, Börje F. Karlsson
Teaching machines to emulate natural handwriting styles remains an open challenge, as it requires synthesizing stroke sequences that dynamically vary in shape, texture, pressure and script - not only across individuals, but also within a single person's handwriting. Attempts at this challenge have largely explored deep learning methods in both online and offline settings. However, these approaches are often constrained by style-specific architectural choices, heavy reliance on large datasets, high compute costs, and a lack of flexible control over writing styles through natural language. To this end, we introduce HandwritingAgent, a language-driven agent that can synthesize natural handwriting sequences directly in Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) format with no need for style-specific training. The agent leverages a large reasoning model to geometrically analyse and autoregressively generate target handwritten glyphs as stroke sequences in a discrete grid canvas environment. Generation is conditioned on texts provided in either conversational or non-conversational mode, along with a reference handwriting-style image. Experiments on diverse handwriting tasks spanning imitation, recognition, multi-lingual handwriting synthesis, and generation of complex handwritten maths and science expressions indicate substantial improvement in performance, with HandwritingAgent matching or surpassing state-of-the-art generative handwriting models, while providing a more efficient, controllable, and generalizable synthesis method.
♻ ☆ Hi-Q: Hierarchical Evidence-guided Query Refinement for Multi-Hop Question Answering NeurIPS 2026
Jueun Kim, Sungho Park, Wook-Shin Han
A central bottleneck in multi-hop Question Answering (QA) is that the granularity at which a question is expressed often differs from the granularity at which corpus evidence is retrievable. Existing methods address this mismatch by imposing fixed graph structures over the corpus, by iteratively reformulating the query, or by executing a generated program over it, but these strategies do not explicitly decide when a query unit is already supported by evidence and when it should be refined. We formulate this bottleneck as retrievable granularity discovery and introduce Hi-Q, an evidence-conditioned framework for hierarchical query refinement. At each query node, a resolution operator tests whether retrieved evidence supports the current query unit; resolved nodes terminate, while unresolved nodes are expanded by a dependency-preserving binary operator and checked by a semantic coverage verifier. Hi-Q therefore grows a query tree whose topology is determined by corpus support signals rather than by a fixed decomposition template or a pre-built graph. We evaluate Hi-Q on three multi-hop QA benchmarks, primarily under full-corpus retrieval, where dependent evidence must be located among open-domain distractors rather than within a small annotated pool. In this setting Hi-Q reaches 52.3 EM and 64.0 F1 averaged over the three benchmarks, ahead of the iterative retrieval baseline IRCoT by 15.1 EM / 18.2 F1 on that same average, and ahead of the graph-based RAG baseline PropRAG by 11.5 EM / 12.0 F1 on MuSiQue-full, without corpus-wide graph construction. In the restricted supporting/distractor setting used by prior work, Hi-Q likewise attains the best accuracy, with 57.9 EM and 69.3 F1 on average, ahead of PropRAG by 5.6 EM / 3.9 F1 and IRCoT by 13.7 EM / 15.8 F1. The project page is available at https://hi-q-project.github.io/.

♻ ☆ Vishing-Tactics-Bench: Forecasting Exploitation Trajectories in Voice Phishing Calls EMNLP 2026
Jeongmin Lee, Dongmyung Sul, Seung Yun, Jinxia Huang
Voice phishing (vishing) unfolds in real time; by the time a call has ended and post-hoc classification is possible, the harm has already been done. The more actionable question is which concrete harm (Information Gathering or Financial Exploitation) an ongoing call is tactically progressing toward. We present Vishing-Tactics-Bench, a benchmark grounded in Endsley's situation-awareness (SA) framework that recasts vishing defense from after-the-fact fraud classification to harm projection: predicting at each turn whether the call will reach either terminal harm. We adapt MITRE ATT&CK to vishing as a 6-tactic taxonomy (Vishing-Tactics) and label 35,340 scammer utterances across 5,645 synthetic Chinese calls. We define Exploitation Trajectory Forecasting, a survival-style protocol over the two terminal harms with three metrics: AP@k, C-index, and divergence error. Baselines ranging from a Markov heuristic to fine-tuned LLMs show that the tactical trajectory serves as an interpretable representation of the call's tactical state, supporting harm-specific forecasting, which can then be used for the downstream application of intervention selection; a stratified lead-time analysis at a tight false-alarm budget further identifies at what point in a call the trajectory signal yields early warning.
comment: Published in Findings of EMNLP 2026. 16 pages
♻ ☆ Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Looped Transformers on Permutation Traversal NeurIPS 2026
Magnus Sesodia, Juil Sock, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt
Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows H hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 17 pages, 12 figures. Code: https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop
♻ ☆ CAMR: Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay for Continual Learning in Large Language Models
Jingpu Yang, Tianhao Li, Fengxian Ji, Yufeng Wang, Shuxin Zheng, Xiaoqing Zhang
Continual learning requires large language models to acquire new knowledge and capabilities while retaining what they have learned. Fine-tuning and replay support acquisition and retention, but deciding whether incoming examples need supervision and which historical examples to revisit remains a challenge. We propose Compatibility-Aware Memory Replay (CAMR), an adaptive framework that jointly controls current-example supervision and historical replay. CAMR combines compatibility checks with a learned memory gate to guide an online policy over three actions: learning incoming examples with general replay, jointly reinforcing compatible related examples, and skipping direct supervision of verified mastered duplicates. The policy learns from acquisition, retention, and training-cost feedback under a bounded per-arrival replay budget. We evaluate CAMR with Qwen3-8B-Base on continual factual updating and cross-task and cross-domain learning. On WikiBigEdit, CAMR consistently leads evaluated methods in Original Match from 3K to 100K facts, reaching 93.66% after just 3K facts and surpassing Full-history Replay (LoRA) after 100K facts. It also achieves the highest final scores on all four selected TRACE tasks and maintains or improves earlier-task performance relative to post-acquisition levels in a sequence spanning financial question answering, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and summarization.
♻ ☆ Beating Hateful Narratives on Social Media with Facts: Retrieval-Augmented Counter-Speech Generation
Greta Damo, Elena Cabrio, Serena Villata
Online hate speech threatens social cohesion by amplifying discrimination and harmful narratives against marginalized communities. While counter-speech (CS) - fact-based, respectful responses to hate - offers a constructive alternative to content removal, its large-scale generation remains constrained by factual reliability and the risk of generic responses. We address these challenges with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in the first large-scale, curated knowledge base built from authoritative international and regional human rights sources, including the United Nations Digital Library, EUR-Lex, and the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights. The framework covers eight groups frequently targeted by online abuse. We systematically evaluate all pipeline components demonstrating that each design choice is empirically motivated, combining automatic metrics, LLM-based judgments, and human evaluation with comparisons against strong baselines. Results show that RAG improves factual grounding, diversity, and perceived effectiveness over No-RAG and performs favorably against existing systems. Our human evaluation further reveals differences between in-group and out-group perceptions of CS, with RAG narrowing but not eliminating this gap. These findings highlight the potential of knowledge grounded CS for scalable social media interventions, while underscoring the need to evaluate such systems with and for the communities they are intended to serve.
♻ ☆ RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Rubric-Driven Review via Agentic Evidence Synthesis and Human-Aligned Generation EMNLP 2026
Shuyu Guo, Wenxiang Hu, Yuyue Zhao, Lun Zhou, Yougang Lyu, Xiaohui Yan, Zhaochun Ren
Peer review at major venues is under unprecedented submission pressure, motivating the use of large language models (LLMs) as review assistants. Existing LLM-based reviewers, however, face two structural limitations. First, they map manuscripts directly to reviews, leaving the underlying rubric implicit and entangling its derivation with the judgement. Second, the prevailing paradigms each capture only half of a good review: training-free agents gather broad evidence but produce undirected critiques, while training-based reviewers inherit human discriminative judgement together with its noise and uneven coverage. We introduce RubricReviewer, a fully rubric-driven framework that addresses both limitations. It makes rubric generation an explicit intermediate step, so that both review generation and the final assessment are conditioned on paper-adaptive rubrics. It further combines a training-free agent (Scout) that gathers external evidence with a human-aligned trained model (Aligner) that consumes this evidence, fusing the strengths of both supervision sources. Experiments on real-world submissions show that RubricReviewer produces reviews that are markedly more comprehensive and more discriminative than prior systems, and exhibits the strongest robustness against adversarial prompt-injection attacks. Ablation studies further confirm the necessity of each component.

♻ ☆ 3D-MoE: Towards Spatial Intelligence with Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Reasoning and Action Generation EMNLP 2026
Yueen Ma, Zenglin Xu, Irwin King
Spatial intelligence, encompassing 3D perception and reasoning, is the essential next frontier of AI. Scaling current 3D vision-language models (VLMs) that rely on dense Transformers for spatial tasks incurs prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we introduce 3D-MoE, a 3D VLM leveraging an efficient mixture-of-experts architecture with a modality- and spatial-context-aware probabilistic routing scheme, stably cultivated by a novel routing curriculum. To seamlessly extend 3D-MoE to embodied AI, we integrate a diffusion-based action head, Pose-DiT, transforming 3D-MoE into a 3D vision-language-action (VLA) model. By employing a rectified flow framework, Pose-DiT generates precise 6D pose actions in a single sampling step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that 3D-MoE achieves superior performance on diverse 3D vision-language benchmarks with drastically fewer activated parameters and yields higher success rates while enabling real-time inference for robot manipulation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/yueen-ma/3D-MoE.

♻ ☆ X-GS: An Extensible Framework for Perceiving and Thinking with 3D Gaussian Splatting EMNLP 2026
Yueen Ma, Zenglin Xu, Irwin King
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a powerful technique for novel view synthesis, subsequently extending into numerous spatial AI applications. However, most existing 3DGS methods operate in isolation, focusing on specific domains. In this paper, we introduce X-GS, an extensible framework that integrates previously isolated 3DGS methods into the perception module of a VLM for spatial tasks, with two major components: the $\textit{Perceiver}$ and the $\textit{Thinker}$. The $\textit{Perceiver}$ performs online 3DGS-based SLAM with semantic distillation and outputs semantic Gaussians from unposed video streams. It leverages recent vision foundation models for stronger geometric priors, and we introduce three novel optimizations to improve semantic distillation efficiency. The $\textit{Thinker}$ interfaces diverse VLMs with these semantic Gaussians, unlocking spatial multimodal capabilities such as 3D visual grounding and scene captioning. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate the efficiency and newly unlocked multimodal capabilities of the X-GS framework. Code is available at https://github.com/yueen-ma/X-GS.

♻ ☆ ResBench: Benchmarking LLM-Generated FPGA Designs with Resource Awareness
Ce Guo, Tong Zhao
Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are widely used in modern hardware design, yet writing Hardware Description Language (HDL) code for FPGA implementation remains a complex and time-consuming task. Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising tool for HDL generation, but existing benchmarks for LLM-based code generation primarily focus on functional correctness while overlooking hardware resource usage. Furthermore, current benchmarks offer limited diversity and do not fully represent the wide range of real-world FPGA applications. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ResBench, the first resource-focused benchmark explicitly designed to distinguish between resource-optimized and inefficient LLM-generated HDL code. ResBench consists of 56 problems across 12 categories, covering applications from finite state machines to financial computing. Our open-source evaluation framework automatically tests LLMs by generating Verilog code, verifying correctness, and measuring resource usage. The experiments, which primarily analyze Lookup Table (LUT) usage, reveal significant differences among LLMs, demonstrating ResBench's capability to identify models that generate more resource-optimized FPGA designs.

♻ ☆ Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization: Teacher in Prompts, Not Gradients
Byung-Kwan Lee, Ximing Lu, Shizhe Diao, Minki Kang, Saurav Muralidharan, Karan Sapra, Andrew Tao, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Ryo Hachiuma
Knowledge distillation transfers a teacher's competence to a small student but is brittle in the small-student regime: forcing the student to imitate logits from a much larger teacher hurts generalization on benchmark families beyond the training corpus. Reinforcement learning (RL) avoids logit imitation by training on the student's own rollouts. However, questions on which every rollout fails yield zero advantage and are silently discarded, and injecting a stronger teacher's response into the policy gradient to recover them breaks the on-policy assumption and induces drift. We introduce Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization (ZPPO), inspired by Vygotsky's zone of proximal development. ZPPO keeps the teacher inside the prompt rather than the policy gradient. On hard questions, where the student's mean rollout accuracy is below half, ZPPO constructs two reformulated prompts. A Binary Candidate-included Question (BCQ) pairs one correct teacher response with one incorrect student response as anonymized candidates the student uses as references. A Negative Candidate-included Question (NCQ) aggregates the student's wrong rollouts into a single prompt to surface their shared failure modes. A prompt replay buffer keeps each hard question eligible for re-sampling until it either graduates (the student's mean rollout accuracy on it reaches half or more) or is FIFO-evicted under finite capacity, amplifying BCQ and NCQ inside the student's current zone of proximal development. We post-train Qwen3.5 students at four scales (0.8B-9B) as VLMs with a 27B teacher and evaluate them on a 31-benchmark suite (16 VLM, 10 LLM, 5 Video); ZPPO outperforms off/on-policy distillation and GRPO, with the largest gains at the smallest scale.
comment: Project page: https://byungkwanlee.github.io/ZPPO-page/
♻ ☆ MindTopo: Can Foundation Models Reason in Topological Space?
Yunfei Ge, Anbang Liu, Qineng Wang, Johnalbert Garnica, Jianwen Lyu, Zihan Wang, Reuben Tan, Jianfeng Gao, Ruohan Zhang, Yining Hong, Jiajun Wu, Manling Li
Spatial reasoning depends not only on metric properties such as distance, angle, and shape, but also on topological relations that remain invariant under continuous deformation. Cognitive science identifies these relations as foundational to spatial understanding, yet foundation-model evaluations largely focus on metric or viewpoint-dependent relations. We introduce MindTopo, a benchmark of topological intuition across five properties grounded in cognitive science and formal topology, namely continuity, separation, order, enclosure, and knots. MindTopo evaluates each property at two cognitive levels. Reasoning asks a model to identify topological relations or infer how they change. Planning instantiates a foundation model as a closed-loop agent whose policy selects environment actions. MindTopo provides a Core Set of 3,900 instances across 13 procedurally generated task types, split into an Easy and a Hard level, and an Extended Set of 11,035 original instances. On the Core Set, we benchmark 13 multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and study agent configurations augmented with image and video generation, covering seven video generative models in planning settings. Every MLLM performs better on reasoning than on planning. On the Easy level, where human scores are available, the strongest model trails humans in both reasoning and planning. On Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct, supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improve reasoning more than planning. Generated observations retain local cues and reach solved endpoints, yet none of the 1,890 evaluated video rollouts passes all process-validity checks.
comment: 93 pages. Revised benchmark with a balanced 3,900-instance Core set, updated model evaluations, expanded video-generation analysis, and clarified Extended evaluation protocol
♻ ☆ Hallucination Mitigation using Agentic AI Natural Language-Based Frameworks
Diego Gosmar, Deborah A. Dahl
Hallucinations remain a significant challenge for Generative AI, undermining trust in AI systems and their reliability. This study investigates how orchestrating multiple specialized AI agents can mitigate hallucinations, with a focus on systems that use Natural Language Processing (NLP) for agent interaction. We design a pipeline that feeds 310 prompts, purposefully crafted to induce hallucinations, into a front-end agent; its outputs are reviewed and refined by second- and third-level agents that detect unverified claims, add explicit disclaimers and clarify speculative content. We introduce four novel Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) - Factual Claim Density, Factual Grounding References, Fictional Disclaimer Frequency and Explicit Contextualization Score - aggregated into a Total Hallucination Score (THS) and assessed by a dedicated fourth-level evaluator agent. Inter-agent context is carried by the Open Floor Protocol (OFP, formerly OVON, Open Voice Network), whose structured JSON messages let each reviewer pass its assessment of hallucination likelihood, and the reasons behind it, to the next stage. Across the 310 prompts, THS improves by a mean of -0.131 per prompt from the front-end agent to the final reviewer (Cohen's d = 2.38), with lower scores on 302 of 310 prompts. The gain is carried mainly by explicit disclaimers and contextualization, making speculative content more transparent and clearly demarcated from factual claims. The results show that multi-agent orchestration with structured, NLP-based exchange of meta-information can substantially strengthen the epistemic framing of AI-generated responses and improve their explainability.

♻ ☆ Do Coding Agents Deceive Us? Detecting and Preventing Cheating via Capped Evaluation with Randomized Tests NeurIPS 2026
Thanawat Lodkaew, Johannes Ackermann, Soichiro Nishimori, Nontawat Charoenphakdee, Masashi Sugiyama, Takashi Ishida
A growing failure mode in agent evaluation and training is that models can achieve high evaluation scores (e.g., test pass rates) by exploiting shortcuts instead of solving the intended task, making these scores deceptive. This makes evaluation scores unreliable as measures of true task-solving ability. We propose CapCode, a framework for constructing coding datasets with randomized tests whose best achievable non-cheating score is deliberately capped below 100%. This capped-score design gives evaluation scores a clearer interpretation: scores substantially above the cap are implausible and therefore provide evidence of cheating. To prevent cheating, we propose CapReward, a reward design based on the CapCode principle to discourage optimization beyond the cap. Experiments across multiple datasets show that CapCode detects cheating while preserving performance ranking of models, and CapReward reduces cheating behavior, yielding models that better follow the intended task specification.
comment: NeurIPS 2026 camera ready version
♻ ☆ Unprompted coordination through shared memory in LLM agents: a locked two-implementation replication and extension
Pekka Abrahamsson, Muhammad Waseem, Esa Karjalainen, Petrus Jussila, Henri Hansen, Jussi Rasku, Bilhanan Silverajan, Kai-Kristian Kemell
Coordination between large language-model agents has become a central question for AI safety and software engineering, as such agents are deployed in groups that share infrastructure. Existing research typically tells the agents that partners exist or asks them to coordinate. Whether coordination arises through shared state alone, with nothing disclosing that anyone else is present, is the key question for deployments that share caches and memory between agents, yet it has rarely been examined, and to our knowledge not with independent replication; this study does both. Four agents each received a short arithmetic task and a key-value store presented to each as its own scratch space; two held complementary halves of one computation, and no prompt mentioned other agents, sharing or collaboration. For reliability, the environment was rebuilt independently from a written protocol, and both implementations ran under hashed locks on design, data and analysis. The results bear novelty value in three respects. Joint success occurred only through the shared store. Whether a model coordinated depended not on its vendor tier but on whether it wrote its intermediate result and looked at the store again, and one ordinary sentence, "check your workspace again before submitting", switched that second look on and off. The findings held under replication. For practice, state shared between agents is a communication channel and should be separated, namespaced and logged. For research, designs should be locked before the data, and the parse rule, endpoint and parameters reported. Future work should test open-weight models and separate using another agent's output from intending to communicate.

♻ ★ SimCT: Recovering Lost Supervision for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation NeurIPS 2026
Jie Sun, Mao Zheng, Mingyang Song, Qiyong Zhong, Yilin Cheng, Bichuan Feng, Pengfei Liu, Junfeng Fang, Xiang Wang
On-policy distillation (OPD) is a standard tool for transferring teacher behavior to a smaller student, but it implicitly assumes that teacher and student predictions are comparable token by token, an assumption that fails whenever the two models tokenize the same text differently. Under heterogeneous tokenizers, exact shared-token matching silently discards a large fraction of the teacher signal at precisely the positions where vocabularies disagree. We propose \textbf{\underline{Sim}ple \underline{C}ross-\underline{T}okenizer OPD (SimCT)}, which restores this signal by enlarging the supervision space: alongside shared tokens, SimCT compares teacher and student over short multi-token continuations that both tokenizers can realize, leaving the OPD loss form itself unchanged. We show that these units are the finest jointly tokenizable supervision interface, and that coarser alternatives remove teacher-student distinctions that are useful for on-policy learning. Across three heterogeneous teacher-student pairs on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, SimCT shows consistent gains over shared-vocabulary OPD and representative cross-tokenizer baselines, with ablations confirming that the improvements come from recovering supervision discarded by exact shared-token matching. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}.

♻ ☆ Understanding When and Where Self-Supervised Speech Models Learn Phonemes and Prosodic Cues through Layer-Wise and Time-Resolved Probing
Masaru Tanibata, Shun Takahashi, Hiroki Ouchi, Sakriani Sakti
Self-supervised speech models (S3Ms) encode a rich hierarchy of acoustic, prosodic, and phonetic information, yet when and where it emerges during pretraining remains unclear. We train frozen-encoder probes on every Transformer layer across pretraining checkpoints of two matched models: HuBERT-Base, whose stage 2 is a separately initialized model trained on new pseudo-label targets, and single-objective wav2vec 2.0-Base. Our five tasks span an acoustic-to-abstract gradient: absolute pitch (F0), speaker-relative pitch, lexical stress, phoneme boundaries, and 38-way phoneme identity. Acoustic-prosodic cues and phone boundaries are decodable from the earliest checkpoints and barely shift across layers, whereas phoneme identity is constructed during pretraining, re-localizing to upper-middle layers under HuBERT's stage-2 targets at a matched update count. Acquisition order therefore tracks abstraction from the acoustic surface, not the segmental/suprasegmental distinction, extending to prosody an account established for phonetic, lexical and syntactic structure; the no-switch wav2vec 2.0 shows no comparable re-localization.
comment: Accepted to SLT 2026
♻ ☆ PersonaFuse: A Situation-Aware Post-Training Framework for Adaptive LLM Behavior in Enterprise Tasks
Yixuan Tang, Yi Yang, Ahmed Abbasi
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in enterprise settings to support task execution and workflow automation. Despite the strong performance of general-purpose models on standard benchmarks, organizations often need to adapt them to domain-specific tasks and operational constraints in practice. However, existing post-training approaches introduce capability trade-offs and lack mechanisms for situational adaptation. In this work, we propose PersonaFuse, a post-training framework that enables situation-aware behavioral adaptation in LLMs. Grounded in Trait Activation Theory and operationalized through the Five-Factor Model, PersonaFuse dynamically adjusts model behavior based on task context using a mixture-of-experts architecture with trait-level experts and a context-aware routing mechanism. We evaluate PersonaFuse at three levels. At the capability level, it achieves balanced improvements across general reasoning, interaction quality, and safety without introducing trade-offs. At the workflow level, it improves task completion in enterprise scenarios involving tool use and structured execution across both B2B and B2C tasks. At the deployment level, we analyze model selection under cost and safety constraints using a capability-cost frontier framework, showing that models adapted with PersonaFuse achieve more favorable trade-offs and are consistently selected as optimal across deployment scenarios. PersonaFuse provides a practical framework for developing LLMs that are not only capable, but also adaptable and deployable in real-world enterprise environments.
♻ ☆ Examining form-based linguistic productivity in people and large language models
Michael Wilson, Robert Frank
Linguistic productivity, as evidenced by the use of words in novel contexts, is one of the most striking facts about human language. However, how abstract the knowledge that enables such productivity is remains unclear. We compare people's and computational language models' linguistic productivity in contexts where successful generalization depends on form-based information. We focus on extending the use of a novel verb learned in the active voice to passive contexts. We find people extend active to passive uses in a way consistent with abstract generalizations concerning linguistic form, even when no plausible meaning can be assigned to the novel verb. In contrast, large language models succeeded only when a meaning like an existing verb's could be assigned to the novel verb. We conclude that computational models' syntactic knowledge remains tied to the distribution and meaning of specific lexical items in a way that human syntactic knowledge is not.
♻ ☆ Unreliable Narrator Framing as a Cost-effective Mechanism for Satire Explanation of Australian and American Satirical News ALT
Kanay Gupta, David Y. Liu, Aditya Joshi
Satirical news is a unique form of misinformation: it is intended to be humorous by the original publication source but can be misinterpreted. Explanation of satirical news articles is challenging because recent and local context needs to be incorporated. This is a pilot study that explores explanation generation for satirical news articles from Australia and compares them alongside those from USA. We show that framing explanations with unreliable narrator theory on open-weight models can be a feasible, cost-effective alternative to frontier models. We find that models identify the satirical tropes more accurately on the American source than the Australian one. This work results in a novel dataset and an evaluation benchmark for satire explanation.

♻ ☆ CAF-Score: Calibrating CLAP with LALMs for Reference-free Audio-Text Alignment Evaluation EACL 2027
Insung Lee, Taeyoung Jeong, HaeJun Yoo, Du-Seong Chang, Myoung-Wan Koo
While Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) have advanced audio understanding and generation, robustly evaluating audio-text alignment remains difficult: reference-based metrics require costly annotations, while Contrastive Language-Audio Pretraining (CLAP)-based reference-free metrics frequently overlook syntactic errors and fine-grained details. We propose CAF-Score, a reference-free metric that calibrates CLAP's coarse-grained semantic alignment with the fine-grained comprehension and syntactic awareness of LALMs. Because CAF-Score scores an audio-text pair symmetrically, one configuration applies to both alignment directions: audio captioning evaluation (the BRACE benchmark) and text-to-audio (TTA) generation evaluation (the RELATE and PAM benchmarks), with a single fusion weight selected once on BRACE and transferred without re-tuning. Across all three human-annotated benchmarks, CAF-Score improves agreement with human judgments over standalone CLAP in the large majority of CLAP-LALM combinations (and in all combinations with the strongest LALM backbone), and outperforms standalone LALM metrics on the main captioning benchmark. It also remains competitive with reference-based metrics in challenging scenarios.

♻ ☆ CRADLE-Dialogue: Expert-Level Crisis Detection in Mental Health Conversations
Grace Byun, Abigail Lott, Rebecca Lipschutz, Sean T. Minton, Elizabeth A. Stinson, Jinho D. Choi
Real-world crisis intervention is inherently conversational, yet existing research largely focuses on static texts. When applied to multi-turn dialogues, current models exhibit significant performance degradation, struggling to track risk signals that emerge as context evolves. To address this gap, we introduce CRADLE-Dialogue, a clinician-annotated benchmark for turn-level crisis detection in conversational settings. The dataset features 600 dialogues with multi-label annotations across clinically grounded risks, including suicide ideation, self-harm, and child abuse, distinguishing past from ongoing risk. We further propose an Alert-Confirm evaluation protocol that distinguishes early warning signals (Alert) from turns where a specific crisis becomes explicitly identifiable (Confirm), reflecting the clinical need to intervene before risk becomes explicit. Experiments show that identifying when risk emerges is much harder than recognizing that it exists: models achieve only mid-40% to high-60% Micro F1. Additionally, we release a synthetic training corpus and a 32B-parameter model that substantially outperforms existing open-source models and achieves competitive or superior results against proprietary models across turn-level, dialogue-level, and confirm-only evaluation settings. We further validate our model on real patient interviews, demonstrating its ability to generalize beyond synthetic conversations.
♻ ☆ K-BrowseComp: A Web Browsing Agent Benchmark Grounded in Korean Contexts
Nahyun Lee, Dongkeun Yoon, Guijin Son, Geewook Kim, Dayoon Ko, Jeonghun Park, Haneul Yoo, Jaewon Cho, Junghun Park, Changyoon Lee, Kyochul Jang, Jaeyeon Kim, Eunsu Kim, Woojin Cho, Seungone Kim
Frontier model evaluations are shifting from foundational capabilities (e.g., instruction following and reasoning) toward compositional, agentic ones, but Korean agentic benchmarks remain scarce. We introduce K-BrowseComp, a web-browsing agent benchmark grounded in Korean contexts, consisting of 400 problems. The 300-problem K-BrowseComp-Verified subset is manually constructed and validated by native Korean speakers. On this subset, frontier LLMs, including GPT-5.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and GLM-5.1, reach only 30.00--45.67\%, a substantial drop from BrowseComp, while Korean LLMs released through Korea's Proprietary AI Foundation Model program obtain only 0.00--10.33\%. We further construct a 100-problem synthetic split using hard few-shot exemplars and failure-mode-targeted generation to exploit the asymmetry between solving and creating web browsing problems. On the adversarially filtered synthetic diagnostic split, the strongest model reaches only 26.00\%, and we report this split separately as a targeted stress test. We publicly release our data and code.
♻ ☆ Why Steering Works: Toward a Unified View of Language Model Parameter Dynamics ACL 2026
Ziwen Xu, Chenyan Wu, Hengyu Sun, Haiwen Hong, Mengru Wang, Yunzhi Yao, Longtao Huang, Hui Xue, Shumin Deng, Zhixuan Chu, Huajun Chen, Ningyu Zhang
Methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), including local weight fine-tuning, LoRA-based adaptation, and activation-based interventions, are often studied in isolation, obscuring their connections and making comparison difficult. In this work, we present a unified view that frames these interventions as dynamic weight updates induced by a control signal, placing them within a single conceptual framework. Building on this view, we propose a unified preference-utility analysis that separates control effects into preference, defined as the tendency toward a target concept, and utility, defined as coherent and task-valid generation, and measures both on a shared log-odds scale using polarity-paired contrastive examples. Across methods, we observe a consistent trade-off between preference and utility: stronger control increases preference while predictably reducing utility. We further explain this behavior through an activation manifold perspective, in which control shifts representations along target-concept directions to enhance preference, while utility declines primarily when interventions push representations off the model's valid-generation manifold. Finally, we introduce a new steering approach SPLIT guided by this analysis that improves preference while better preserving utility. Code is available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit/blob/main/examples/SPLIT.md.
